title: Bash Control Flow: Tests, Loops & Case
summary: A dense field guide to Bash branching and iteration — the difference between [ and [[, arithmetic evaluation with (( )), for/while/until loops, case pattern matching, and the correct way to read a file line by line. Covers mechanics, quoting traps, exit-status semantics, and the mistakes that silently corrupt scripts.

chapters.title: Exit Status: The Engine Behind Every Branch
points: Every command returns an exit status: 0 = success/true, non-zero (1-255) = failure/false — inverted vs C and most languages
`$?` holds the exit status of the last foreground command; it is overwritten by the very next command, so capture it immediately: `rc=$?`
`if` does not test an expression — it runs a command and branches on that command's exit status
`if grep -q root /etc/passwd; then ...` is idiomatic: no `[` needed when a command already answers the question
`true` and `false` are real commands (builtins) returning 0 and 1 respectively
`test`, `[`, and `[[` are all just ways to produce an exit status; `[` is a command whose last argument must be `]`
`[` is a POSIX builtin in Bash but also exists as `/usr/bin/[` — proof it is a normal command, not syntax
`&&` runs the right side only if the left returned 0; `||` runs it only if the left returned non-zero
`cmd1 && cmd2 || cmd3` is NOT if/else: if cmd2 fails, cmd3 also runs — a classic silent bug
`!` negates the status of a pipeline: `if ! command -v git; then echo missing; fi`
Exit status of a pipeline is the status of the LAST command; `set -o pipefail` makes it the first failing one
`set -e` aborts on non-zero, but is suppressed inside `if`, `while`, `&&`, `||`, and `!` conditions — this is why tests do not kill the script
128+N encodes death by signal N: 130 = SIGINT (Ctrl-C, 128+2), 137 = SIGKILL (128+9)
Exit status 127 = command not found; 126 = found but not executable
Trap for `set -e`: a function whose last command returns non-zero makes the function return non-zero — an unintended failure

chapters.title: test and [ ]: The POSIX Workhorse
points: Syntax: `[ EXPR ]` — spaces around `[` and `]` are mandatory; `[$x = 1]` is a command-not-found error
String tests: `-z STR` (empty), `-n STR` (non-empty), `STR1 = STR2` (equal), `STR1 != STR2`
Numeric tests: `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge` — these are for numbers only; `=` and `!=` are for strings
`[ 10 -gt 9 ]` is true; `[ 10 \> 9 ]` compares as strings and is FALSE ("1" < "9")
File tests: `-e` exists, `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-L` symlink, `-r/-w/-x` permissions, `-s` size > 0
`-e` follows symlinks; `-L` does not — a broken symlink is `-L` true but `-e` false
Comparison operators for files: `-nt` (newer than), `-ot` (older than), `-ef` (same inode/hardlink)
Combining: POSIX-portable form uses `[ a ] && [ b ]`, not `[ a -a b ]` — `-a`/`-o` are deprecated and ambiguous
THE core gotcha: unquoted empty variable collapses the word — `[ $x = y ]` with x empty becomes `[ = y ]`, a syntax error
Always quote in `[ ]`: `[ "$x" = "y" ]` — quoting is not optional, it is load-bearing
Legacy defensive idiom `[ "x$x" = "xy" ]` predates reliable quoting; still seen in old scripts
`[ "$x" = "-n" ]` can misparse in ancient shells because the value looks like an operator
No globbing, no regex: `[ "$f" = *.txt ]` compares against the literal string `*.txt`
`[ ]` performs word splitting and glob expansion on unquoted variables — a variable containing `a b` becomes two arguments
Use `[ ]` when the script must run under `sh`/dash/POSIX; use `[[ ]]` when the shebang is `#!/bin/bash`

chapters.title: [[ ]]: Bash's Safer Conditional Keyword
points: `[[ ]]` is a shell KEYWORD, not a command — Bash parses it specially, so normal expansion rules are suspended inside
No word splitting, no glob expansion on variables: `[[ $x = y ]]` is safe even when x is empty or contains spaces
Quoting still matters on the RIGHT side: `[[ $f == *.txt ]]` globs; `[[ $f == "*.txt" ]]` is a literal match
Pattern matching with `==`/`!=`: `[[ $name == a* ]]` matches any name starting with a
Regex with `=~`: `[[ $ip =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]` — ERE, not PCRE, and must be UNQUOTED to act as a regex
Capture groups land in the `BASH_REMATCH` array: `${BASH_REMATCH[0]}` = whole match, `[1]` = first group
Store complex regex in a variable and use it bare: `re='^v[0-9]+'; [[ $tag =~ $re ]]` — avoids quoting hell
Logical operators inside: `&&`, `||`, and parentheses for grouping — `[[ -f $f && -r $f ]]`
`<` and `>` do lexicographic string comparison without escaping (unlike `[ ]` where they must be `\<`)
Still uses `-eq`/`-lt` for numbers, but `(( ))` is the better choice for arithmetic
`[[ ]]` does not do arithmetic on comparison: `[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is FALSE (string compare) — a top-3 real-world bug
Comparison table: `[ ]` = portable/POSIX/needs quotes; `[[ ]]` = Bash-only/no splitting/regex/globs; `(( ))` = arithmetic
`[[ ]]` cannot be used where a command is needed dynamically (e.g. as an argument to `find -exec`)
Empty-variable safety demo: `x=''; [ $x = a ]` errors, `[[ $x = a ]]` cleanly returns false

chapters.title: Arithmetic: (( )) and $(( ))
points: `(( expr ))` evaluates arithmetic and sets exit status: result 0 (numeric zero) means status 1 (FALSE) — inverted, memorize it
`$(( expr ))` is arithmetic EXPANSION: substitutes the numeric result into the command line
Inside `(( ))` variables need no `$`: `(( i < n ))` works; `$` is allowed but noisy
Integer only — `$(( 7 / 2 ))` is 3, and `$(( 1.5 ))` is a syntax error; use `bc -l` or `awk` for floats
Modulo of a negative truncates toward zero: `$(( -7 % 3 ))` is -1, not 2
Leading zero means OCTAL: `$(( 010 ))` is 8 — bites date arithmetic like `08` and `09` (invalid octal digits, hard error)
Fix octal: strip with `${x#0}` or force base with `$(( 10#$x ))`
`let 'x = 1 + 2'` and `declare -i x` are older alternatives; `(( ))` is the modern idiom
`set -e` trap: `(( i++ ))` when i was 0 returns status 1 and kills the script; use `(( i++ )) || true` or `(( ++i ))`
Post-increment vs pre-increment matters for exit status, not just value — `((i++))` returns the OLD value's truthiness
Comparison chaining works: `(( a < b && b < c ))` — real logical operators, unlike `[ ]`
Overflow wraps at 64-bit signed; no error is raised
Idiomatic guard: `if (( count > 0 )); then` reads better and is safer than `[ "$count" -gt 0 ]`

chapters.title: for Loops: Lists, Globs, C-Style
points: Word-list form: `for x in a b c; do echo "$x"; done` — iterates over words after expansion
`for f in *.txt; do` is glob iteration and is SAFE with spaces in filenames — unlike `for f in $(ls)`
Never parse `ls`: `for f in $(ls)` word-splits on spaces and breaks on newlines in names
Empty glob gotcha: with no matches, `*.txt` stays literal and the loop runs once with the pattern itself; guard with `[[ -e $f ]]` or `shopt -s nullglob`
Array iteration: `for x in "${arr[@]}"` — quotes and `[@]` are both required; `${arr[*]}` joins into one word
Positional args: `for arg in "$@"` (or bare `for arg; do`, which defaults to `"$@"`)
Brace expansion ranges: `for i in {1..10}`, with step `{0..20..5}`, zero-padded `{01..12}` — literal, cannot use variables
`{1..$n}` does NOT work — brace expansion happens before parameter expansion; use C-style or `seq`
C-style form: `for (( i=0; i<n; i++ )); do` — arithmetic context, no `$` needed, best for counters
Line-based iteration is wrong with for: `for line in $(cat f)` splits on every space, not per line
`break` exits the loop; `continue` skips to the next iteration; both take a level count: `break 2` exits two nested loops
`for` over command output with `IFS` control: `IFS=$'\n'` narrows splitting to newlines but still globs — still inferior to `while read`
Loops are compound commands: you can redirect the whole loop — `for ...; do ...; done > out.txt` opens the file once
`for` returns the exit status of the last command executed in the body; empty list = status 0

chapters.title: while and until: Condition-Driven Loops
points: `while CMD; do ...; done` repeats while CMD exits 0; `until CMD` repeats while CMD exits non-zero
The condition is a command list — `while [[ $i -lt 5 ]]`, `while (( i < 5 ))`, or `while ping -c1 host` all valid
Arithmetic loop: `i=0; while (( i < 5 )); do echo $i; (( i++ )); done`
`while true; do ...; done` and `while :; do ...; done` are infinite loops; `:` is the no-op builtin
Retry-with-backoff pattern: `n=0; until cmd; do (( ++n >= 5 )) && exit 1; sleep $(( 2 ** n )); done`
Polling pattern: `while ! nc -z host 5432; do sleep 1; done` — wait for a service
Multi-command condition: only the LAST command's status decides — `while cmd1; cmd2; do` branches on cmd2
`until` is `while !` — pick whichever reads positively; avoid double negatives
The infinite-loop bug: forgetting to mutate the counter, or mutating a copy inside a subshell
`break`/`continue` work identically to for loops, with the same numeric level argument
`while read` is the canonical file/stream loop (next chapter) — it consumes stdin, which conflicts with commands inside the body
Loop can be fed by process substitution: `while read x; do ...; done < <(cmd)` keeps the body in the current shell
Consuming stdin trap: `ssh`, `ffmpeg`, and `mysql` inside a `while read` loop eat the input; fix with `ssh -n` or `< /dev/null`
`sleep` in a tight polling loop is mandatory — a bare `while ! test; do :; done` pins a CPU core at 100%

chapters.title: case: Pattern Dispatch
points: Syntax: `case $var in pattern) cmds ;; pattern2) cmds ;; *) default ;; esac`
`$var` needs no quotes in `case` — no word splitting happens in the case word (same protection as `[[ ]]`)
Uses glob patterns, NOT regex: `*` any string, `?` one char, `[abc]` char class, `[!abc]` negated
Alternation with `|`: `start|begin|up) ...;;` matches any of them
First matching pattern wins; there is no fallthrough by default and no `break` needed
`*)` is the catch-all default and must be LAST — a `*)` in the middle makes everything after it dead code
`;;` ends a branch; `;&` falls through to the NEXT branch's body unconditionally (Bash 4+)
`;;&` continues testing subsequent patterns — lets multiple branches match one value
`shopt -s nocasematch` makes case (and `[[ ]]`) matching case-insensitive
Classic use: argument parsing — `case $1 in -h|--help) usage ;; -v) verbose=1 ;; -*) die "unknown $1" ;; esac`
Classic use: init-script dispatch — `case $1 in start) ...;; stop) ...;; restart) stop; start ;; esac`
Prefer `case` over long `if/elif` chains on one variable: flatter, faster to read, harder to get wrong
Patterns are matched literally against the expanded word — quoting a pattern (`"*"`) makes it a literal asterisk
Exit status is that of the last command in the matched branch; 0 if nothing matched
Extended globs (`shopt -s extglob`) add `@(a|b)`, `?(x)`, `*(x)`, `+(x)`, `!(x)` to case patterns

chapters.title: Reading a File Line by Line
points: The one correct idiom: `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`
`IFS=` (empty) prevents `read` from stripping leading and trailing whitespace from the line
`-r` prevents backslash interpretation — without it, `C:\path` loses its backslashes and `\` at EOL joins lines
The `IFS=` prefix applies only to the `read` command, not the whole script — no cleanup needed
`read` returns non-zero at EOF, which is what terminates the loop
Last-line trap: a file with no trailing newline still sets `line`, but `read` returns 1 — fix with `while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n $line ]]`
Split into fields: `while IFS=: read -r user pass uid rest; do` — extra fields all land in the last variable
Read from a command: `cmd | while read ...` puts the loop in a SUBSHELL, so variable changes are lost after the loop
Fix the subshell: use `while read ...; done < <(cmd)` (process substitution) or `shopt -s lastpipe`
`read -t SECONDS` adds a timeout; `read -n N` reads N chars; `read -d ''` reads until NUL
NUL-safe file lists: `find . -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do` handles newlines in filenames
Read into an array in one shot: `mapfile -t lines < file` (aka `readarray`) — faster, whole file in memory
`while read` is slow for large files (one syscall-ish per line); for pure text transforms reach for `awk`/`sed`
Redirect the loop, not each command: `done < file` opens the file once and is the only place the input belongs
Nested read from a second file needs a separate descriptor: `read -u 3` with `exec 3< other.txt`

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Missing spaces: `if [$x -eq 1]` — `[$x` is not a command; always `[ $x -eq 1 ]`
`=` vs `==` vs `-eq`: `=` string (POSIX), `==` string (Bash), `-eq` numeric — mixing them silently compares wrong
`[ "$a" == "$b" ]` works in Bash but is not POSIX; under `dash` it errors
Unquoted variable in `[ ]` with an empty value = "unary operator expected" error
`[[ 10 > 9 ]]` false; `(( 10 > 9 ))` true — never string-compare numbers
Pipe-to-while subshell: `count=0; grep x f | while read l; do ((count++)); done; echo $count` prints 0
`for f in $(ls)` breaks on spaces; `for f in *` is correct
Unquoted `$f` in the loop body re-splits it: always `"$f"`
`(( i++ ))` returning 1 under `set -e` aborts the script
Leading-zero octal: `(( 08 + 1 ))` is "value too great for base"
`case` with a `*)` branch placed before specific patterns swallows everything
Missing `;;` merges two case branches into a syntax error at the next `)`
Forgetting `-r` on `read` mangles paths and escapes
Body commands stealing stdin inside `while read` — loop exits after one iteration
`if cmd > /dev/null` tests cmd's status, not its output — to test output use `[[ -n $(cmd) ]]`
Run `shellcheck` — it catches nearly every item on this list mechanically

chapters.title: Summary: Choosing the Right Construct
points: Branch on a command's success → plain `if cmd`, no brackets at all
POSIX/sh portability → `[ ]` with every variable quoted
Bash string, glob, or regex test → `[[ ]]`, unquoted right side for patterns
Any numeric comparison or math → `(( ))` / `$(( ))`, never `[ ]`'s `-lt` unless portability forces it
Iterate a known list, glob, or array → `for`, with `"${arr[@]}"` quoted
Iterate a counter → C-style `for (( i=0; i<n; i++ ))`
Loop until a condition flips → `while` / `until` with a `sleep` in polling loops
Dispatch on one value against many patterns → `case`, catch-all `*)` last
Read a file or stream by line → `while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`
Need loop variables to survive → avoid pipes into loops; use `< <(cmd)` or `mapfile`
Whole-file into memory → `mapfile -t arr < file`
Defensive header for real scripts: `set -euo pipefail` plus `IFS=$'\n\t'`
Truthiness recap: exit 0 = true everywhere EXCEPT inside `(( ))`, where numeric 0 = false
Quoting rule of thumb: quote everything except a glob/regex pattern on the right of `[[ ]]` and the word in `case`
Verify with `bash -n script.sh` (syntax check), `bash -x script.sh` (trace), and `shellcheck` (lint)
